docs.title: neuromem
docs.text:
Long-term memory for AI agents. neuromem records past conversations, consolidates them in the background (a "dream cycle"), and gives the agent a compact, dated view of what it remembers before each answer.

The library ships two memory models:

Not merged yet

EpisodicMemory, the neuromem-episodic benchmark agent and the official judge are on the episodic-memory-v2 branch and are not yet in main.

Episodic memory Tag-graph memory Unit of memory One conversation session, with its date One conversation session What is embedded The whole memory (date, summary, transcript) LLM-extracted tag labels Hierarchy Every node of agglomerative dendrograms from several linkages, so memories belong to many overlapping episodes Recursive HDBSCAN over tag vectors Cluster summaries Dated history that leads with the current state Paragraph summary plus a one-word name Near-duplicates Merged in the dream cycle, all dates kept Not merged Status Experimental (ADR-005) Default NeuroMemory

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
uv sync --dev

Episodic memory:

from neuromem import EpisodicMemory
from neuromem_gemini import GeminiEmbeddingProvider, GeminiLLMProvider

memory = EpisodicMemory(
    GeminiLLMProvider(api_key="...", model="gemini-3.8-flash"),
    GeminiEmbeddingProvider(api_key="...", model="gemini-embedding-2"),
    db_path="memory.db",
)
memory.enqueue_session(
    [{"role": "user", "text": "I keep my old sneakers in a box under the bed."},
     {"role": "assistant", "text": "Noted."}],
    timestamp="2023/01/02 (Mon) 10:00",
)
# ... more sessions ...
memory.dream()
context = memory.build_context("Where are my old sneakers?", today="2023/05/30")
print(context.text)

Tag-graph memory:

from neuromem import NeuroMemory, SQLiteAdapter, ContextHelper
from neuromem_gemini import GeminiEmbeddingProvider, GeminiLLMProvider

memory = NeuroMemory(
    storage=SQLiteAdapter("memory.db"),
    llm=GeminiLLMProvider(api_key="..."),
    embedder=GeminiEmbeddingProvider(api_key="..."),
)
memory.enqueue("I graduated with a Business Administration degree last year.")
memory.force_dream(block=True)
print(ContextHelper(memory).build_prompt_context("What degree did I get?"))

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
neuromem is long-term memory for LLM agents. Conversations go in, get consolidated in the background, and come back out as a compact context block the agent can read. This page describes how the code is laid out, how the two memory models work, how agents use them, and how the benchmark harness measures them.

The design decisions behind this layout are recorded in the ADRs:

ADR Decision ADR-001 Hand-rolled numpy clustering (later superseded in part by ADR-003) ADR-002 Centroids get placeholder labels at clustering time and LLM names later ADR-003 HDBSCAN clustering, per-centroid paragraph summaries, expand_node tool ADR-004 All LLM work moves to the background dream cycle; retrieval makes no LLM calls ADR-005 Episodic memory: dated whole-session memories and overlapping episode clusters

Each provider package ships its own prompt files under prompts/ (generate_summary.prompt, extract_tags_batch.prompt, generate_junction_summaries_batch.prompt and so on). Prompt wording is therefore a provider concern, not a core concern. The exception is EpisodicMemory, which owns its prompts in episodic.py and calls the provider's free-form complete(prompt).

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
neuromem-core has three layers. Orchestration code depends only on the contract layer. Concrete providers and storage are passed in through constructors.

  • Contracts: packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/providers.py defines EmbeddingProvider (get_embeddings), LLMProvider (summaries, tags, named entities, category names, junction summaries, complete) and ClusteringProvider (cluster) plus the Cluster record. packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/storage/base.py defines StorageAdapter, an ABC with 16 abstract methods covering memory rows, nodes, edges, nearest-node search, subgraph walks, decay and the access-weight spike.
  • Orchestration: system.py (NeuroMemory) runs the tag-graph pipeline. episodic.py (EpisodicMemory) runs the episodic pipeline. context.py (ContextHelper) and tools.py turn stored memory into text for an agent.
  • Adapters: storage/sqlite.py (SQLiteAdapter) and clustering.py (HDBSCANClusteringProvider, StubClusteringProvider) ship in core. LLM and embedding providers live in sibling packages.

NeuroMemory.__init__ checks each injected object with isinstance against its ABC and raises TypeError on a mismatch. On LLMProvider only generate_summary, extract_tags and generate_category_name are abstract. The batch methods default to looping over the single-item method, and extract_named_entities and generate_junction_summary also have defaults, so a provider can start with the three abstract methods and add the rest later. LLMProvider.complete raises NotImplementedError by default; all four shipped LLM providers implement it.

docs.title: Two memory models
docs.text:
Two memory models now exist side by side in neuromem-core. Both are exported from neuromem/__init__.py. They share the provider contracts but not storage or retrieval.

NeuroMemory (tag graph) EpisodicMemory (episodes) ADRs 001 to 004 005 Unit stored A text, or a session transcript via enqueue_session A session transcript with its date and session id What gets embedded Short LLM-extracted tag labels The whole memory: date, summary and transcript Hierarchy HDBSCAN over tag vectors, recursive scipy agglomerative dendrograms over memory vectors, several linkages Storage Any StorageAdapter (default SQLiteAdapter) Its own SQLite tables (ep_memories, ep_episodes) Consolidation trigger Background thread when the inbox reaches dream_threshold, or force_dream Explicit, blocking dream() Retrieval output ASCII tree of centroids, tags and memory snippets Dated text: episodes, memory summaries, raw transcripts Dates Not passed in Parsed, sorted on, rendered and fed to every prompt Decay and LTP Yes No

docs.title: NeuroMemory: the tag graph
docs.text:
NeuroMemory in packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/system.py stores memories as rows and builds a graph of tag nodes (leaves), centroid nodes (clusters of tags) and edges. A memory links to its tags with has_tag edges. A centroid links to its children with child_of edges, weighted by the cluster's cohesion (mean pairwise cosine of its members).

Constructor defaults:

Parameter Default Effect dream_threshold 10 Inbox size that starts a background dream cycle decay_lambda 3e-7 per second Exponential decay rate of access_weight archive_threshold 0.1 Memories whose decayed weight falls below this are archived cluster_threshold 0.65 Validated and stored, but not read by the default HDBSCAN provider clusterer HDBSCANClusteringProvider() Pluggable clustering (ADR-003)

enqueue(raw_text, metadata) inserts a row with an empty summary and returns its id. It makes no LLM call. If the inbox count is at or above dream_threshold and no cycle is running, it starts a daemon thread named neuromem-dream. enqueue_session(turns) joins the turns as role: text blocks separated by blank lines and calls enqueue with the result.

_run_dream_cycle takes a non-blocking lock, so a second concurrent cycle returns immediately. Its steps:

  1. Read every inbox memory and set them to dreaming.
  2. _backfill_summaries: call llm.generate_summary_batch on memories without a summary and persist with set_summaries.
  3. llm.extract_tags_batch over the summaries.
  4. llm.extract_named_entities_batch and set_named_entities. Entities annotate the rendered rows; they do not feed clustering.
  5. _ensure_tag_nodes: embed only labels not already stored, in one get_embeddings call, and upsert them as leaf nodes.
  6. _run_clustering: pass every node in the label map to clusterer.cluster, then write each returned cluster as a centroid with a placeholder label (cluster_ plus the first 12 characters of the node's UUID) and child_of edges.
  7. Insert has_tag edges from each memory to its tag nodes.
  8. _run_all_centroid_naming: pass every centroid whose label still starts with cluster_ to resolve_centroid_names.
  9. _run_all_junction_summarisation: pass every centroid without a paragraph_summary to resolve_junction_summaries.
  10. storage.apply_decay_and_archive.
  11. Set the batch to consolidated.

Steps 8 and 9 catch their own exceptions and log them, so a naming or summary failure does not fail the cycle. On any other exception the batch goes back to inbox and the exception is re-raised. Only the status change is undone. Summaries, named entities, nodes and edges written before the failure stay in storage; the next cycle reuses the stored summaries.

HDBSCANClusteringProvider L2-normalises the embeddings, runs hdbscan.HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=2, metric="euclidean", allow_single_cluster=True), emits one Cluster per label (noise points stay unclustered leaves) and recurses on the new centroids while a level produces at least two clusters, up to depth 8. Clusters come back children first, and _run_clustering raises ValueError if a provider breaks that order.

Decay is computed in SQLiteAdapter.apply_decay_and_archive as access_weight * exp(-decay_lambda * t), where t is the time since last_accessed (or created_at). Archiving a memory deletes its has_tag edges, so it drops out of retrieval. retrieve_memories resets access_weight to 1.0 for consolidated memories (long-term potentiation, LTP).

docs.title: EpisodicMemory: dated episodes
docs.text:
EpisodicMemory in packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/episodic.py has no tags. A memory is a whole session. ADR-005 gives the reasons: on the tag pipeline's seed-42 LongMemEval run most misses were not retrieval misses, dates never reached the system, summaries dropped assistant-side details, and memories appeared under several tags.

Constructor defaults: db_path=":memory:", linkages=("average", "ward"), merge_threshold=0.97, max_episode_size=30, embed_chunk_chars=24_000, workers=16.

enqueue and enqueue_session take timestamp and session_id. The timestamp is parsed by parse_session_date, which accepts the LongMemEval format (2023/05/20 (Sat) 02:21) and several ISO forms. Dated memories sort by timestamp; undated ones sort after all dated ones in insertion order. No LLM call happens on enqueue.

dream() holds an RLock for the whole cycle and blocks the caller:

  1. _summarise_and_embed: summarise each inbox memory in parallel with MEMORY_SUMMARY_PROMPT, which receives the session date and asks for relative dates to be resolved to absolute ones. Embed Date + Summary + Transcript. The transcript is split into chunks so that each chunk plus its Date and Summary header fits in embed_chunk_chars (at least 1,000 transcript characters per chunk). Chunk vectors are normalised and averaged.
  2. _merge_near_duplicates: union-find over pairs with cosine similarity at or above merge_threshold. Each group becomes a unit whose canonical id is its earliest member. A unit with more than one member gets a merged summary from MERGE_PROMPT, regenerated only when its member set changes.
  3. _rebuild_episodes: for each linkage, build the full scipy dendrogram over unit embeddings (cosine distance, or Euclidean on normalised rows for ward). Every internal node with at least 2 and at most max_episode_size members becomes an episode; identical member sets across linkages are kept once. Episodes are keyed by a SHA-1 of their sorted memory ids. Existing keys are reactivated without an LLM call. New keys get a summary from EPISODE_PROMPT in a fixed TOPIC / CURRENT / HISTORY format, plus two vectors: the embedding of the summary text and the normalised mean of the member embeddings.

An LLM failure or empty response in any of these steps falls back to deterministic text (the truncated transcript, or the concatenated records) through _complete_or, so one bad call does not fail the cycle. Other errors roll back uncommitted SQLite writes and re-raise. Each step commits when it finishes, so completed steps are kept and the next dream() redoes the rest.

build_context(query, today=...) embeds the query once and scores units and active episodes by dot product with the normalised query vector. Defaults: top_memories=12, top_episodes=6, raw_memories=3, raw_chars=12_000, episode_embedding="summary" (or "mean", "max"), max_episode_overlap=0.8. An episode is skipped if its Jaccard overlap with a higher-ranked chosen episode exceeds 0.8. The rendered text has four parts: today's date, the chosen episodes, the chosen units in date order with their dates, and the raw transcripts of the closest units. It returns an EpisodicContext that also lists the memory, session and episode ids it used, which the benchmark uses for evidence recall.

docs.title: Hot path and background work
docs.text:
ADR-004 splits NeuroMemory into a hot path that serves agent turns and a background path that does all LLM work.

  • Hot path: enqueue is one insert plus a count. ContextHelper.build_prompt_context makes one embedder call. expand_node makes no embedder call. retrieve_memories makes no model calls. None of them call the LLM once the dream cycle has finished.
  • Background: the dream cycle does summarisation, tagging, entity extraction, label embedding, clustering, naming and junction summaries.

Memories only gain has_tag edges inside the dream cycle, so a memory in inbox cannot be reached by retrieval. In an agent this means the current session lives in the model's chat history and memory holds earlier sessions.

resolve_centroid_names and resolve_junction_summaries still run inside build_prompt_context and expand_node. They return early when no node in the subgraph has a placeholder label or a missing summary. Otherwise they log a WARNING that the ADR-004 invariant is broken and do the work on the hot path. Naming makes one batched generate_category_names_batch call and persists with update_node_labels. Summarising makes one generate_junction_summaries_batch call per tree level, children before parents, and persists each level with update_junction_summaries. If batched naming fails, each centroid takes the label of the child closest to its embedding (ADR-002). If batched summarising fails or returns an empty summary, llm.generate_junction_summary is called for the affected centroids (ADR-003). Both public methods catch and log any exception, so rendering never fails because of them. The dream cycle calls them with flags that suppress the warning.

EpisodicMemory does not follow this split yet. Its dream() is synchronous and must be called by the owner before build_context will see new memories. build_context itself makes one embedder call and no LLM calls.

docs.title: Agent integration
docs.text: There are three ways for an agent to use NeuroMemory.

docs.title: Passive injection
docs.text: ContextHelper.build_prompt_context(task, top_k=5, depth=3) in context.py builds the context block. It embeds the task, takes the top_k nearest nodes with storage.get_nearest_nodes (a single numpy cosine pass over all nodes), walks get_subgraph to depth hops, caps the result at 80 nodes with _enforce_node_cap (seed nodes are never dropped; other nodes are ranked by hop distance from the nearest seed over child_of edges and the farthest are dropped, along with memories that lose all their tags) and renders an ASCII tree with _render_ascii_tree. Memory snippets are capped at 300 characters and junction summaries at 400. It returns an empty string when nothing is found.

docs.title: Tool functions
docs.text:
The functions in tools.py take the NeuroMemory instance as an argument so a wrapper can bind it:

Function Defaults Behaviour search_memory(query, system, top_k=5, depth=2) depth 2 Calls build_prompt_context with these arguments retrieve_memories(memory_ids, system) Returns full rows including raw_content; unknown ids are skipped; consolidated rows get the LTP spike expand_node(node_id, system, depth=2) depth clamped to 5 Renders the subtree under one node with the same 80-node cap; no query embedding, no LTP

docs.title: Google ADK
docs.text:
neuromem_adk.enable_memory(agent, db_path, ...) in packages/neuromem-adk/src/neuromem_adk/enable.py wires all of this into a Google ADK Agent in place and returns the NeuroMemory:

  • Providers default to GeminiLLMProvider and GeminiEmbeddingProvider, built from GOOGLE_API_KEY or GEMINI_API_KEY. Either can be overridden. cluster_threshold and dream_threshold are forwarded only when given.
  • before_model_callback gets build_before_model_context_injector: it takes the current user text, calls build_prompt_context, and appends the tree to llm_request.config.system_instruction.
  • after_agent_callback gets build_after_agent_turn_capturer: it enqueues the user text and the latest assistant text as two memories with role and turn metadata.
  • Three tools are appended to agent.tools: search_memory_tool, retrieve_memories_tool, expand_node_tool. They are plain wrapper functions so ADK's schema generator does not see the system argument.
  • Existing callbacks are kept: _chain_callback turns the slot into a list with neuromem's callback last. A second call on the same agent raises ValueError.

NeuromemMemoryService in memory_service.py implements ADK's BaseMemoryService. add_session_to_memory enqueues every text event and then calls force_dream(block=True); search_memory parses memory ids out of the rendered tree and returns them as MemoryEntry objects. enable_memory does not install it.

EpisodicMemory has no tool functions or ADK wiring yet. The benchmark calls it directly.

docs.title: Benchmark harness
docs.text: neuromem-bench runs published memory benchmarks against interchangeable agents. LongMemEval is the only dataset loader so far.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text: datasets/base.py defines BenchTurn, BenchSession (with timestamp), BenchInstance (question, gold answer, question type, metadata) and the Dataset ABC. datasets/longmemeval.py (LongMemEval) downloads longmemeval_s_cleaned.json, longmemeval_m_cleaned.json or longmemeval_oracle.json from the xiaowu0162/longmemeval-cleaned Hugging Face dataset into ~/.cache/neuromem-bench/ (or NEUROMEM_BENCH_CACHE). Each instance keeps its haystack session ids and dates, and stores question_date and answer_session_ids in metadata.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
agent.py defines the BaseAgent protocol: process_session(turns, *, timestamp, session_id), answer(question, *, question_date), reset().

Agent Memory Answer path NullAgent Last 50 turns One Gemini call with the turns in the system prompt NaiveRagAgent One embedding per turn Top 5 turns by cosine similarity NeuromemAgent NeuroMemory, dream_threshold=9999, cluster_threshold=0.55 force_dream, then build_prompt_context(top_k=20), then one Gemini call NeuromemAdkAgent enable_memory with the same thresholds force_dream, then an ADK Runner with the injector and three tools NeuromemEpisodicAgent EpisodicMemory with gemini-embedding-2 dream(), then build_context(today=question_date), then one Gemini call with prompts/episodic_answer.prompt

NeuromemAgent and NeuromemAdkAgent ignore session timestamps and the question date. NeuromemEpisodicAgent passes both through. The answer model for the one-shot agents is GeminiAnsweringClient in _client.py. _providers.py builds the memory-side provider pair for gemini, openai, anthropic or gemma.

docs.title: Runner
docs.text: runner.py (run_benchmark) calls _run_one_instance for each instance: reset, process_session for each session in order, answer, then _score_prediction. Agents may expose last_trace and last_tool_calls; these are copied into the result row. If the trace has retrieved_session_ids, _evidence_recall records the fraction of the instance's answer sessions that reached the context. A metric exception keeps the prediction and records metric_error. With workers > 1 each thread builds its own agent from agent_factory. Results stream to JSONL and a Markdown summary with a per-question-type table is written next to it.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: metrics.py has exact_match, contains_match (normalised substring), llm_judge (a generic single-prompt judge) and longmemeval_judge. longmemeval_judge uses the per-type judge prompts copied from LongMemEval's official evaluator: separate templates for temporal reasoning (off-by-one days allowed), knowledge update (the updated answer must be present), preference (rubric) and abstention (instance ids containing _abs). It runs at temperature 0 and counts a verdict as correct when it contains "yes". The default judge model is gemini-3.8-flash.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
packages/neuromem-bench/scripts/run_longmemeval.py selects agents (null, naive-rag, neuromem, neuromem-adk, neuromem-episodic), the metric (--metric llm-judge uses longmemeval_judge), --judge-model, --per-type-sample N with --seed for a stratified reproducible sample, --workers and --rpm. All Gemini clients on one API key share one token bucket. scripts/rescore_with_llm_judge.py re-judges an existing JSONL with the official prompts without re-running the agent.

Differences from the official protocol, which every comparison below should account for:

  • Sample. neuromem's numbers come from 60 questions (10 per type) or fewer, not all 500. The six types are equally weighted, which matches the "unweighted mean of six types" some vendors report, not question-weighted accuracy over 500 questions (where single-session-user and multi-session dominate).
  • Judge. The prompts are the official ones, but the judge is gemini-3.8-flash, not gpt-4o-2024-08-06. Changing only the judge model moved the tag-graph score by about one question in 59.
  • Answer model. gemini-3.8-flash is a 2026 model. The official baselines use gpt-4o (2024). The table below shows the answer model alone moving a system by more than 10 points.
  • Interval. 15 of 16 has a 95% interval of 0.72 to 0.99.

The episodic result is 16 instances, not stratified by type (6 of the 16 are multi-session), so it cannot yet be placed against any row below. The tag-graph result (0.746 on a balanced 59) is a rough match for the mid-table systems in shared-protocol re-runs. A full 500-question run with the official GPT-4o judge would be needed to place it properly.

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text: These numbers do not form one leaderboard. The answer model alone moves a single memory system by 10 points or more: Mastra Observational Memory scores 84.23% with gpt-4o and 94.87% with gpt-5-mini, and Hindsight ranges from 83.6% to 91.4%. Judges also differ. The official protocol uses gpt-4o-2024-08-06 with per-type prompts, while other rows use gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini, GPT-OSS-120B, Gemini, gpt-5.4, the answering model itself, or a judge they don't name. Mnemon's results show that changing only the grader shifts its score by 1 to 2 points. The way scores are combined also varies: Mastra, SimpleMem and Redis average the six question types without weighting, which gives a different number from per-question accuracy, and one study reports token F1, which cannot be compared with any judged accuracy. Most of the top scores are self-reported by vendors. Shared-protocol re-runs put several of them lower: on OmniMemEval, Zep scores 79.8, Mem0 56.0 and Hindsight 72.2, against self-reported 90.2, 94.4 and 94.6. Part of each gap comes from the weaker common answer model, so it is not all inflation. The dataset variant also matters. The oracle file holds only the evidence sessions and scores much higher (GPT-4o 87.0% on oracle vs 60.6% on S), M is harder, several vendor pages don't say which variant they used, and OmniMemEval uses the cleaned S data released after the 2024 paper results. The ChatGPT/Coze pilot and the Mem-alpha subset use different question sets and histories, so they should not be compared with any S row. The fairest comparisons are within one source that holds the answer model and judge fixed: the Redis table (gpt-4o answering and judging), OmniMemEval (gpt-4.1-mini answering, gpt-4o-mini judging) and EvalMem (gpt-4o-mini answering, gpt-5-mini judging).

docs.title: Episodic memory (EpisodicMemory)
docs.text:
EpisodicMemory is the second memory model in neuromem-core (packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/episodic.py, ADR-005). It runs alongside the tag-graph model and is selected in the benchmark with --agent neuromem-episodic.

Not merged yet

EpisodicMemory, the neuromem-episodic benchmark agent and the official judge are on the episodic-memory-v2 branch and are not yet in main.

The idea in one paragraph: record every conversation as one memory with its date, embed the whole memory, and cluster the memories hierarchically so the same memories can be grouped in many ways at many levels of abstraction. Each cluster (an episode) gets an LLM summary written as a dated history that leads with the current state, so a cluster about "where I keep my sneakers" reads like an episodic memory: what changed, when, and what is true now.

docs.title: Why a second model
docs.text:
A review of the tag-graph model on LongMemEval found that most wrong answers were not retrieval failures. The relevant memory was usually in the prompt. The answer was wrong because:

  • no dates reached the system, so "how many days ago" and "what is my current X" could not be answered;
  • short, user-centric summaries dropped details the assistant had given;
  • the same memory was rendered under several tags, using about a third of the context on duplicates;
  • centroid vectors were averages of 1 to 4 word tag labels, which drift towards generic meanings.

The episodic model removes tags entirely and makes dates first-class.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S["Session turns + date + session id"] --> E["enqueue_session(): no LLM calls"]
    E --> I[("ep_memories, status = inbox")]

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Storage is a self-contained SQLite database (:memory: by default, or a file path). Two tables:

erDiagram
    ep_memories {
        TEXT id PK "mem_<12 hex>"
        TEXT session_id
        TEXT session_date "as given, e.g. 2023/05/20 (Sat) 02:21"
        REAL sort_key "epoch seconds; undated = 1e12 + insertion order"
        TEXT raw_content "full transcript, role: text per turn"
        TEXT summary "dated LLM summary"
        BLOB embedding "float32, L2-normalised"
        TEXT merged_into "canonical memory id if merged, else NULL"
        TEXT unit_summary "merged summary, on the canonical row only"
        TEXT unit_key "hash of the member set unit_summary was built from"
        TEXT status "inbox | consolidated"
        TEXT metadata "JSON"
    }
    ep_episodes {
        TEXT id PK "ep_<12 hex>"
        TEXT member_key UK "sha1 of sorted member memory ids"
        TEXT member_ids "JSON list of unit ids, date order"
        TEXT first_date
        TEXT last_date
        TEXT summary "TOPIC / CURRENT / HISTORY"
        BLOB summary_embedding "embedding of the summary text"
        BLOB mean_embedding "normalised mean of member embeddings"
        INTEGER active "1 if produced by the latest dream"
    }
    ep_memories ||--o{ ep_memories : "merged_into"
    ep_episodes }o--o{ ep_memories : "member_ids"

A unit is the thing that gets clustered: a canonical memory plus any near-duplicates merged into it. Most units contain one memory.

docs.title: Ingest
docs.text:
enqueue_session(turns, timestamp=None, session_id=None, metadata=None) joins the turns as role: text paragraphs and stores one row in the inbox. It makes no LLM or embedding call, so it is safe on a request path.

Dates are parsed from the formats used by chat logs and LongMemEval (2023/05/20 (Sat) 02:21, ISO 8601 and a few others). The parsed time becomes sort_key. Undated memories sort after all dated ones, in insertion order.

docs.title: Dream cycle
docs.text: dream() runs the whole consolidation synchronously under a lock. If any step raises, the database transaction is rolled back so the next cycle starts from a clean state. A failed or empty LLM call does not abort the cycle: that one summary falls back to the raw records (or the transcript head for memory summaries) and a warning is logged.

docs.title: 1. Dated memory summaries
docs.text:
Each new memory is summarised with one LLM call (MEMORY_SUMMARY_PROMPT), in parallel across workers threads. The prompt gets the session date and must:

  • start with "On YYYY-MM-DD (Day),";
  • convert every relative time expression into an absolute date, keeping the original phrase in brackets ("on 2023-05-13 (last Saturday)");
  • keep every personal fact: possessions, purchases, places, people, amounts, counts, durations, preferences, plans and changes of mind;
  • state changed values explicitly ("The user now keeps X in Y");
  • keep the concrete specifics the assistant gave: names, numbers, list items with their numbers, steps, moves;
  • run 3 to 10 sentences depending on content.

docs.title: 2. Whole-memory embeddings
docs.text:
Each memory is embedded as:

Date: 2023-05-20 (Sat)
Summary: <dated summary>

Transcript:
<full transcript>

Embedding APIs silently truncate long input: both gemini-embedding-001 and gemini-embedding-2 accept a 40,000-character input without an error. So any text longer than embed_chunk_chars (24,000 characters, about 6,000 tokens) is split into chunks. Each chunk carries the same date and summary header, the chunk vectors are L2-normalised and averaged, and the average is normalised again. The default embedder is gemini-embedding-2, which takes about 8,000 tokens per input.

gemini-embedding-2 is multimodal: given a plain list of strings it returns one embedding for the whole list. GeminiEmbeddingProvider therefore wraps each text in its own Content so it gets one vector per text from every model.

docs.title: 3. Near-duplicate merging
docs.text:
Memories whose embeddings have cosine similarity at or above merge_threshold (0.97) are merged. Pairs above the threshold are joined with union-find, so merging is transitive. The earliest memory in each group becomes the canonical id, and the others get merged_into set.

A merged unit gets one LLM summary (MERGE_PROMPT) that keeps every fact and date, orders events by date, and states the latest value first where values changed. The summary is rebuilt whenever the unit's member set changes, which is detected by comparing unit_key with a hash of the current member ids.

In the rendered context a merged unit appears once, with all its dates, for example [2023-01-01 (Sun), 2023-02-01 (Wed)] mem_….

docs.title: 4. Many overlapping clusterings
docs.text:
For each linkage method in linkages (default average and ward), scipy builds the full agglomerative dendrogram over the unit embeddings:

  • average, complete, single and weighted use cosine distance on L2-normalised vectors;
  • ward uses Euclidean distance on the same normalised vectors, which ranks the same as cosine distance.

Every internal node of every dendrogram becomes a candidate episode. Identical member sets from different linkages are kept once. Sets larger than max_episode_size (30) are skipped, because a summary of 30+ sessions turns generic and the prompt gets slow.

With N units and two linkages there are up to 2(N - 1) episodes. A memory belongs to one episode per dendrogram level above it, so it sits in many episodes at different granularities. The two linkages disagree in useful ways: average linkage tends to chain related topics together, while Ward produces compact, balanced groups.

graph TD
    subgraph average["average linkage"]
        A1["ep: sneakers + shoe rack"] --> m1["mem 2023-01-02: sneakers under bed"]
        A1 --> m2["mem 2023-03-04: moved sneakers to rack"]
        A2["ep: home organisation"] --> A1
        A2 --> m3["mem 2023-02-10: closet clear-out"]
    end
    subgraph ward["ward linkage"]
        W1["ep: closet + sneakers"] --> w3["mem 2023-02-10"]
        W1 --> w2["mem 2023-03-04"]
        W2["ep: home organisation"] --> W1
        W2 --> w1["mem 2023-01-02"]
    end

In this example "home organisation" has the same member set in both trees, so it is stored once; the two lower episodes differ and both are kept.

docs.title: 5. Episode summaries
docs.text:
Each new episode is summarised from its members' summaries, oldest first, each prefixed with its dates (EPISODE_PROMPT). The output format is fixed:

TOPIC: Where the user keeps their old sneakers
CURRENT: As of 2023-03-04 the user keeps their old sneakers on the shoe rack by
the front door; before that (2023-01-02) they were in a box under the bed.
HISTORY:
- 2023-01-02: Keeps old sneakers in a box under the bed.
- 2023-02-10: Cleared out the closet, donated two pairs of boots.
- 2023-03-04: Moved the sneakers to the new shoe rack by the front door.

The prompt also tells the model to name each distinct item when several of the same kind appear, which helps counting questions.

Episodes are cached by member_key, a hash of the sorted member memory ids (not unit ids). A later dream cycle that produces the same set reactivates the stored episode without an LLM call. A set that changed, including a unit that gained a merged memory, gets a new summary.

Each episode stores two vectors:

Vector What it is Good for summary_embedding Embedding of the episode summary text Matching the query against the words the answering model will read mean_embedding Normalised mean of the member memory embeddings Pure geometry, no dependence on summary quality

Summing member vectors instead of averaging them gives a vector with the same direction, so it ranks identically under cosine similarity and is not offered as a separate option.

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
build_context(query, today=None, ...) makes one embedding call and no LLM calls.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent
    participant M as EpisodicMemory
    participant E as Embedder
    A->>M: build_context(question, today=question_date)
    M->>E: embed(question)
    E-->>M: q
    M->>M: score every unit: cos(q, unit vector)
    M->>M: score every active episode: cos(q, summary or mean vector)
    M->>M: take top episodes, skipping overlap > 0.8 Jaccard
    M->>M: take top units, sort chosen units by date
    M-->>A: text + memory, session and episode ids

Scoring:

  • Units are ranked by cosine similarity between the query and the unit vector (the normalised mean of its members). The top top_memories (12) are kept.
  • Episodes are ranked by episode_embedding: "summary" (default), "mean" or "max" (the better of the two). Walking down the ranking, an episode is skipped if its member set overlaps an already chosen one by more than max_episode_overlap (0.8, Jaccard), so the context does not fill with near-identical parent and child episodes. The top top_episodes (6) are kept.

The rendered context has four parts:

Today's date: 2023-05-30 (Tue)

## Episodes
### Episode ep_… (3 memories: 2023-01-02 (Mon), 2023-02-10 (Fri), 2023-03-04 (Sat))
TOPIC: …
CURRENT: …
HISTORY: …

## Memories
The most relevant individual memories, oldest first.
[2023-01-02 (Mon)] mem_…: On 2023-01-02 (Mon), the user …
[2023-03-04 (Sat)] mem_…: On 2023-03-04 (Sat), the user …

## Transcripts
### mem_… (2023-03-04 (Sat))
user: …
assistant: …

The transcripts section holds the full text of the raw_memories (3) closest units, each capped at raw_chars (12,000 characters). It is there for questions about exact details, especially what the assistant said.

The result also lists the memory ids, session ids and episode ids used, which the benchmark uses to compute evidence recall.

docs.title: Answering
docs.text:
The benchmark agent (NeuromemEpisodicAgent) puts the context into episodic_answer.prompt with these rules:

  • compute elapsed time from the memory dates to today's date (the question date), not the real current date;
  • the most recent dated statement of a changed fact is the current one;
  • for "how many" questions, list each distinct item with its date, remove duplicates, then count, and do not count the subject of the question;
  • quote exact details from the transcripts for questions about what the assistant said;
  • say so when the memory does not contain the answer or contradicts the question's premise.

docs.text: Setting Default Where linkages ("average", "ward") EpisodicMemory merge_threshold 0.97 cosine EpisodicMemory max_episode_size 30 units EpisodicMemory embed_chunk_chars 24,000 characters EpisodicMemory workers 16 threads (agent uses 24) EpisodicMemory top_memories 12 build_context top_episodes 6 build_context raw_memories / raw_chars 3 / 12,000 build_context episode_embedding "summary" build_context max_episode_overlap 0.8 Jaccard build_context LLM gemini-3.8-flash NeuromemEpisodicAgent Embedder gemini-embedding-2 NeuromemEpisodicAgent Request timeout 180 s NeuromemEpisodicAgent

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Per dream cycle with N new memories:

  • N memory-summary calls;
  • one merge call per merged unit whose membership changed (rare);
  • one episode call per new member set, up to len(linkages) × (N − 1) on the first cycle (about 60 to 75 for a 50-session LongMemEval instance after de-duplication and the size cap);
  • one or two batched embedding calls.

Retrieval costs one embedding call. On LongMemEval_S instances (about 50 sessions each) the first dream cycle took 400 to 600 seconds with 8 workers on gemini-3-flash-preview; the worker count was raised to 24 for the full benchmark.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Chunks or sessions as the unit. A memory is currently a whole session. Embedding a whole session averages over everything said in it, so a brief aside (where the user keeps their sneakers, mentioned during a recipe chat) has little weight in the vector. Splitting sessions into chunks before clustering would let that aside cluster with other sneaker mentions. It would also multiply the number of units and episodes by roughly ten. A cheaper middle ground is to keep sessions as the memory but store one vector per chunk and score a memory by its best chunk. Evidence recall from the benchmark (the share of answer sessions that reached the prompt) decides whether either is needed.

Incremental cost. Every dream cycle rebuilds the dendrograms from scratch. Episode summaries are cached by member set, but adding one memory changes the member set of every ancestor in the tree, so each new memory triggers about log N to N new episode summaries.

Storage contract. The model uses its own SQLite tables, not the StorageAdapter contract. Adopting it as the main model would need memory embeddings and episode records in that contract.

docs.title: Benchmark results
docs.text:
All results are on LongMemEval_S (Wu et al., ICLR 2025). Each question comes with a chat history of about 50 sessions (about 115K tokens). The agent reads the history session by session, then answers one question about it.

The head-to-head run is incomplete and not stratified

Both head-to-head runs stopped at 10:48 UTC on 2026-11-25, when the Gemini project reached its monthly spending cap. Before that, 16 instances finished validly for both agents. The numbers below are those 16 paired instances. They are not a balanced sample: 6 are multi-session questions, 3 knowledge-update, 3 single-session-user, 2 temporal-reasoning, 1 single-session-assistant and 1 preference. The page will be updated when the full 60-instance runs complete.

Not merged yet

EpisodicMemory, the neuromem-episodic benchmark agent and the official judge are on the episodic-memory-v2 branch and are not yet in main.

docs.title: The judge
docs.text:
Earlier runs used one generic prompt ("is the prediction correct?") on gemini-2.0-flash-001, a model that has since been retired. The harness now uses the official LongMemEval prompts, copied verbatim from src/evaluation/evaluate_qa.py:

  • Abstention questions (ids ending in _abs) are correct if the model says the information is not available.
  • Temporal reasoning does not penalise off-by-one errors in day counts.
  • Knowledge update accepts an answer that mentions the old value as long as it gives the updated one.
  • Preference questions are graded against a rubric, not an exact answer.

Rescoring the existing seed-42 run with the official prompts changed 8 of 59 verdicts. Some false negatives became correct (for example "Your sister gave you…" against the gold "my sister") and some false positives became wrong (7 days against a gold of 18). The judge model matters too: the same predictions score 0.729 with gemini-2.5-flash as judge and 0.746 with gemini-3.8-flash.

docs.title: Sample size
docs.text: Ten questions per type is small. The 95% Wilson interval for 44 correct out of 59 is 0.62 to 0.84, and for a single type at 6 out of 10 it is 0.31 to 0.83. Differences of a few points between runs are noise. Comparisons below are paired: both agents answer the same instances.

Same 16 instances, same model (gemini-3.8-flash) for memory and answers, same judge.

Per type, on the paired instances:

Question type n Episodic Tag-graph knowledge-update 3 1.00 0.67 multi-session 6 1.00 0.83 single-session-assistant 1 1.00 0.00 single-session-preference 1 0.00 0.00 single-session-user 3 1.00 1.00 temporal-reasoning 2 1.00 1.00

The three questions only the episodic agent got right show the mechanisms at work:

Question Gold Episodic Tag-graph How many sessions of the bereavement support group did I attend? (knowledge update) five "5 sessions (noted on October 30, 2023, updating your earlier mention of 3 sessions on May 11, 2023)" "three" What percentage of leadership positions do women hold in my company? (multi-session) 20% "20% (20 out of 100 total positions)" "the exact percentage … isn't recorded" What was the average framerate improvement with the Hardware-Aware Modular Training agent? (assistant detail) about 20% quotes the transcript: "approximately 20%" describes the paper, no number

The first needs dates to pick the newer value. The second needs two facts from different sessions. The third needs the raw transcript, because the detail was in what the assistant said.

A 3-to-0 split on discordant pairs is not statistically significant (McNemar exact p ≈ 0.25). The full 60-instance run is needed before drawing a conclusion.

The comparison is between two whole systems, not two clustering methods. The episodic agent also receives session and question dates, gets the raw transcripts of its three closest memories (the tag agent sees only summaries), uses gemini-embedding-2 instead of gemini-embedding-001, and has a different answer prompt. Nothing here shows how much of the gain comes from the episodes themselves; a run with top_episodes=0 would isolate that.

All 23 episodic instances that finished before the cap (including 7 with no valid tag-graph pair) scored 22 of 23. No LLM call fell back to degraded text in either run before the cap.

docs.title: Tag-graph memory (NeuroMemory)
docs.text:
This page describes the original neuromem memory model, NeuroMemory, step by step. It covers the data model, ingestion, every step of the dream cycle, retrieval, the agent tools and the tunable defaults. The pipeline, retrieval, tools and defaults sections are taken from the code in:

  • packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/system.py (NeuroMemory)
  • packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/context.py (ContextHelper)
  • packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/clustering.py (HDBSCANClusteringProvider)
  • packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/vectors.py
  • packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/tools.py
  • packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/storage/sqlite.py (SQLiteAdapter)
  • packages/neuromem-gemini/src/neuromem_gemini/llm.py and the templates in packages/neuromem-gemini/src/neuromem_gemini/prompts/
  • packages/neuromem-adk/src/neuromem_adk/enable.py and callbacks.py

The benchmark and limitations sections draw on the documents they link to. The episodic model that runs alongside it is described in episodic-memory.md and ADR-005.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A memory is a piece of raw text, usually a whole conversation session. An LLM summarises it and extracts short tags from the summary ("degree", "Acme Corp", "task management"). Each distinct tag becomes a leaf node with an embedding of the tag text. HDBSCAN clusters the tag vectors into a hierarchy of centroid nodes, and an LLM names each centroid with one word and writes a short paragraph about what sits under it. Memories link to their tag nodes.

At query time the query is embedded, the nearest nodes (tags or centroids) are found, the graph is walked outward from them, and the result is rendered as an indented text tree that goes into the answering model's prompt.

The expensive work happens in a background dream cycle. Ingestion only writes a row.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
SQLiteAdapter creates three tables (_SCHEMA_DDL in storage/sqlite.py). Foreign keys are switched off (PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF), so edge endpoints are not checked by the database. The database runs in WAL mode.

erDiagram
    MEMORIES ||--o{ EDGES : "has_tag (source)"
    NODES ||--o{ EDGES : "has_tag (target)"
    NODES ||--o{ EDGES : "child_of (source = parent)"
    NODES ||--o{ EDGES : "child_of (target = child)"

    MEMORIES {
        text id PK "mem_ plus 32 hex"
        text raw_content "NOT NULL"
        text summary "empty until dream step 2"
        text status "inbox, dreaming, consolidated, archived"
        real access_weight "default 1.0"
        integer last_accessed "NULL until retrieved"
        integer created_at "insert time, Unix seconds"
        text metadata "JSON or NULL"
        text named_entities "JSON list, default empty"
    }
    NODES {
        text id PK "node_ plus uuid4"
        text label "tag text or centroid name"
        blob embedding "float32 bytes"
        integer embedding_dim "corruption check"
        integer is_centroid "0 leaf, 1 centroid"
        text paragraph_summary "centroids only, NULL until summarised"
    }
    EDGES {
        integer id PK
        text source_id
        text target_id
        real weight
        text relationship "has_tag or child_of"
    }

docs.title: memories
docs.text:
One row per ingested text. id is mem_ followed by 32 hex characters. created_at is the time of insertion (int(time.time())), not the date of the conversation. summary is written as an empty string at insert time and filled in by the dream cycle. named_entities is a JSON list of strings.

status has four values, enforced by a CHECK constraint:

Status Meaning Set by inbox Ingested, not yet processed insert_memory; also the rollback target dreaming Claimed by a running dream cycle Step 1 of the dream cycle consolidated Processed, linked into the graph, subject to decay Last step of the dream cycle archived Decayed below the threshold; tag edges removed apply_decay_and_archive

access_weight starts at 1.0. Decay lowers it; retrieval resets it to 1.0.

docs.title: nodes
docs.text:
One row per tag (leaf) or centroid. id is node_ followed by a hyphenated UUID4. The embedding is stored as raw float32 bytes with its dimension in embedding_dim. The first node written fixes the dimension for the whole table: upsert_node rejects any embedding of a different length, and logs a warning above 4096 dimensions. On read, a blob whose length is not embedding_dim * 4 raises StorageError.

paragraph_summary holds the centroid's 2 to 4 sentence summary. An upsert of an existing node id sets it back to NULL.

docs.title: edges
docs.text:
Relationship Source Target Weight has_tag memory id node id (normally a leaf tag) 1.0 child_of parent centroid id child node id cluster cohesion (mean pairwise cosine of the children)

(source_id, target_id, relationship) is unique and insert_edge uses INSERT OR IGNORE, so repeating an edge is a no-op. Indexes exist on memories(status), edges(source_id) and edges(target_id).

docs.title: enqueue(raw_text, metadata=None)
docs.text:
NeuroMemory.enqueue makes no LLM call.

  1. Rejects empty raw_text with ValueError.
  2. Inserts a row with status='inbox', summary='', access_weight=1.0, last_accessed=NULL. Metadata must be JSON-serialisable.
  3. Counts inbox rows. If the count is at least dream_threshold (default 10) and is_dreaming is false, it starts a daemon thread named neuromem-dream that runs _run_dream_cycle.
  4. Returns the memory id.

docs.title: enqueue_session(turns, metadata=None)
docs.text: Takes a list of dicts with role and text keys (other keys are ignored). It validates the list, builds one transcript with "{role}: {text}" per turn joined by blank lines, and calls enqueue once. A session becomes a single memory. There is no timestamp parameter, so the session date is not stored.

docs.title: force_dream(block=True)
docs.text:
• block=True: if a background dream thread is alive, join it, then run _run_dream_cycle on the caller's thread.
  • block=False: if a background thread is alive, return. Otherwise start a new daemon thread.

Only one cycle can run at a time. _run_dream_cycle takes _dream_lock without blocking and returns at once if another cycle holds it.

docs.title: The dream cycle
docs.text:
NeuroMemory._run_dream_cycle runs these steps in this order.

flowchart TD
    A["Acquire _dream_lock (non-blocking)"] -->|held| Z0["Return, no-op"]
    A -->|acquired| B["Step 1: Read all inbox memories"]
    B -->|none| Z1["Release lock, return"]
    B --> C["Flip batch to dreaming"]
    C --> D["Step 2: Summary backfill (generate_summary_batch)"]
    D --> E["Step 3: Tag extraction (extract_tags_batch)"]
    E --> F["Step 4: NER (extract_named_entities_batch), write named_entities"]
    F --> G["Step 5: Tag nodes: embed new labels, upsert leaves"]
    G --> H["Step 6: HDBSCAN recursive clustering, write centroids and child_of edges"]
    H --> I["Step 7: Wire has_tag edges"]
    I --> J["Step 8: Name placeholder centroids"]
    J --> K["Step 9: Junction summaries, floor-up"]
    K --> L["Step 10: Decay and archive consolidated memories"]
    L --> M["Step 11: Flip batch to consolidated"]
    M --> Z2["Release lock"]
    D -. exception .-> R["Flip batch back to inbox, re-raise"]
    E -. exception .-> R
    F -. exception .-> R
    G -. exception .-> R
    H -. exception .-> R
    I -. exception .-> R
    L -. exception .-> R
    R --> Z2

Steps 8 and 9 catch and log their own exceptions, so a naming or summary failure does not roll the cycle back.

docs.title: Step 1: claim the batch
docs.text: storage.get_memories_by_status("inbox") returns every inbox row ordered by created_at, then id. If there are none the cycle returns. Otherwise one UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...) sets them all to dreaming. Memories enqueued after this point stay in the inbox for the next cycle.

docs.title: Step 2: summary backfill
docs.text:
_backfill_summaries selects memories whose summary is empty or whitespace (rows that already have a summary are skipped). It calls llm.generate_summary_batch on their raw_content. If the number of summaries returned differs from the number of inputs it raises ValueError, which triggers the rollback. Results are written with set_summaries and copied onto the in-memory dicts used by later steps.

Gemini (GeminiLLMProvider.generate_summary_batch):

  • One text goes to generate_summary (prompt generate_summary.prompt).
  • Up to 6 texts go in one call; more are split into chunks of 6 (_MEMORY_SUMMARY_BATCH_CHUNK_SIZE) and run on a thread pool of up to 10 workers (_BATCH_WORKERS).
  • Each chunk uses generate_summary_batch.prompt, which numbers the texts [1], [2] and asks for a JSON array of strings. Raw text has \n# replaced by \n first, so it cannot inject Markdown headings into the prompt.
  • If the response is not valid JSON or has the wrong length, every item in the chunk is summarised with a single call. An empty or non-string item is redone with a single call.

The prompts ask for 2 to 4 sentences that keep personal facts about the user, proper nouns, numbers and dates, and implied facts, and that prefer personal facts over generic advice.

docs.title: Step 3: tag extraction
docs.text:
llm.extract_tags_batch(summaries) returns one list of tag strings per memory.

Gemini (extract_tags_batch):

  • One summary goes to extract_tags (comma-separated output, extract_tags.prompt).
  • Two or more go in one call with no chunking (extract_tags_batch.prompt), asking for a JSON array of arrays with 5 to 12 tags of 1 to 4 words each.
  • Parse failure or a length mismatch falls back to one extract_tags call per summary. A non-list inner element falls back for that item.
  • Each tag is stripped of whitespace and surrounding quotes. Lists are cut to 12 tags.

Tags keep the casing the model returns. They are matched to existing nodes by exact string, so "Degree" and "degree" are different tags.

docs.title: Step 4: named-entity extraction
docs.text:
llm.extract_named_entities_batch(summaries) returns proper nouns per memory (brands, products, places, people, organisations). set_named_entities writes them to the named_entities column straight away, before the remaining steps.

Gemini uses the same shape as tag extraction: a single unchunked call with extract_named_entities_batch.prompt, per-item fallback to extract_named_entities, and a cap of 8 entities. The single-item prompt returns NONE for no entities, which becomes an empty list.

Entities are not used for clustering or retrieval. They appear only on the annotation line of the rendered tree and in retrieve_memories results.

docs.title: Step 5: tag node creation and embedding
docs.text:
_ensure_tag_nodes:

  1. Collects the union of tag strings across the batch.
  2. Loads every node in storage with get_all_nodes (leaves and centroids, ordered by id) into a dict keyed by label. When two nodes share a label, the one with the later id wins.
  3. Finds the labels not already in that dict, sorts them, and embeds them in one embedder.get_embeddings call. The Gemini embedder (default model gemini-embedding-001) sends at most 100 texts per request.
  4. Upserts each as a leaf (is_centroid=False) with id node_<uuid4>.

It returns the label dict, which now holds every node in storage plus the new leaves. A tag that matches an existing label, including a centroid's label, reuses that node.

docs.title: Step 6: HDBSCAN recursive clustering
docs.text:
_run_clustering passes every node in the label dict, as (id, embedding) pairs, to self.clusterer.cluster. That includes centroids from earlier cycles, not only the new leaves. With fewer than 2 nodes it does nothing.

HDBSCANClusteringProvider._cluster_level then runs, starting at depth 0:

  1. Stop if depth is 8 or more (_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH) or there are fewer than min_cluster_size (2) inputs.
  2. L2-normalise each embedding, so Euclidean distance orders points the same way as cosine distance.
  3. Run hdbscan.HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=2, metric="euclidean", allow_single_cluster=True).fit_predict.
  4. Drop points labelled -1 (noise). Noise points get no parent at this level and are not passed up.
  5. For each cluster, emit a Cluster with:
  6. id c_ plus 16 hex characters,
  7. embedding = mean of the members' original (not normalised) embeddings,
  8. child_ids = the member ids,
  9. cohesion = mean cosine similarity over all member pairs.
  10. If this level produced at least 2 clusters, recurse on the cluster centroids at depth + 1.

Clusters are emitted children first, so a single forward pass can write them. For each cluster _run_clustering:

  1. Creates a centroid node node_<uuid4> with is_centroid=True, the cluster embedding, and a placeholder label cluster_ followed by characters 5 to 16 of the node id (the first 12 characters of the UUID, which always include the hyphen at position 8).
  2. Writes a child_of edge from the centroid to each child, with weight equal to the cohesion. Child ids that start with c_ are mapped to the storage id created earlier; if one has not been seen yet, it raises ValueError (a provider ordering bug).

Old centroids and their edges are never deleted, and an existing centroid never gains new child_of edges. Because every node, including leaves and older centroids, is clustered again each cycle, each cycle writes a new set of centroids over the whole graph, and a node can collect several parents across cycles.

cluster_threshold (default 0.65) is validated and stored on NeuroMemory but the HDBSCAN provider does not read it. random_state (default 42) is stored by the provider but not passed to HDBSCAN.

docs.title: Step 7: has_tag wiring
docs.text: For each memory and each of its tag strings, insert_edge(memory_id, node_id, 1.0, "has_tag"), where node_id comes from the label dict. Memories link to the node whose label matches the tag exactly. No step links a memory to a centroid ancestor. A memory is linked to a centroid only when one of its tags equals that centroid's label (see step 5).

docs.title: Step 8: centroid naming
docs.text:
_run_all_centroid_naming loads all nodes, keeps centroids whose label starts with cluster_, and calls resolve_centroid_names(placeholders, expected_placeholders=True, all_nodes=...).

For each placeholder centroid:

  1. Children: get_subgraph([centroid_id], depth=1) and keep the targets of child_of edges whose source is the centroid. A centroid with no children is skipped.
  2. Input: the labels of the first 20 children.
  3. avoid_names: the labels of every centroid not in the set being named, skipping empty labels and labels that still start with cluster_.
  4. Batched call: llm.generate_category_names_batch(groups, avoid_names=...). If it raises or returns the wrong number of names, the whole batch goes to the fallback.
  5. First word: each returned name is cut to its first whitespace-separated word. An empty name sends that centroid to the fallback.
  6. Nearest-child fallback: _nearest_child_label returns the label of the child whose embedding has the highest cosine similarity to the centroid embedding. If the centroid has no embedding or a zero vector, it returns the first child's label.
  7. Persist: update_node_labels writes all new labels in one transaction.

Gemini (generate_category_names_batch):

  • Groups go in chunks of 30 (_BATCH_CHUNK_SIZE) on up to 10 workers. One group uses the single-call prompt.
  • generate_category_names_batch.prompt asks for one lowercase English noun per group, bans generic nouns ("thing", "aspect", "topic" and others), asks for distinct names within the batch, and includes the avoid line.
  • render_avoid_section sorts the avoid labels alphabetically, keeps the first 30 (_AVOID_NAMES_MAX), and renders Avoid reusing these already-taken labels: a, b, c.
  • Each name is cleaned to its first token, stripped of punctuation and lowercased. A non-string item, a name in _GENERIC_LABEL_BLOCKLIST or an empty name is redone with the single-call prompt. A chunk whose response is not valid JSON or has the wrong length is redone one group at a time with the single-call prompt. If the single-call prompt also returns an empty or blocked name, the result is the first word of the first concept, lowercased, or concept if there are none.
  • avoid_names is a hint only. A returned name that is in the avoid set is accepted.

The nearest-child fallback gives a centroid the exact label of one of its children, and nothing stops two centroids from getting the same name. In the next cycle the label dict in step 5 keeps only one node per label, so one of the two same-named nodes is left out of clustering and of tag matching.

docs.title: Step 9: junction (paragraph) summaries, floor-up
docs.text:
_run_all_junction_summarisation collects every centroid whose paragraph_summary is NULL or empty and calls resolve_junction_summaries(dirty, expected_unsummarised=True). Centroids that already have a summary are not regenerated, even if new memories have since been linked to the tags under them.

Levels: _group_by_level orders the dirty centroids so children are summarised before parents. For each dirty centroid it finds which of its child_of children are also dirty. Level 0 is the dirty centroids with no dirty children; it removes them and repeats. If no centroid is ready (a cycle in the graph), the rest go in one final level.

Snippets: for each centroid in a level, _gather_child_snippets builds one string per child:

  • Centroid child: its paragraph_summary, or its label if it has none.
  • Leaf child: Memories tagged '<label>': s1 | s2 | s3, using up to 3 non-empty summaries of non-archived memories linked by has_tag. A leaf with no linked memories contributes its label.

Summarise: llm.generate_junction_summaries_batch(groups) produces one summary per centroid. If it raises or returns the wrong count, the code calls llm.generate_junction_summary once per group. An empty result for one slot is also redone with generate_junction_summary. Results are written with update_junction_summaries, one transaction per level, before the next level reads them.

LLMProvider.generate_junction_summary in the base class joins the snippets with spaces after cutting each to 120 characters. Gemini overrides it with an LLM call, so with Gemini every fallback is another model call.

Gemini batches 8 groups per call (_JUNCTION_BATCH_CHUNK_SIZE) on up to 10 workers. generate_junction_summaries_batch.prompt asks for 2 to 4 fact-dense sentences per group that keep personal facts and proper nouns, returned as a JSON array. Snippets have \n# replaced by \n.

docs.title: Step 10: decay and archive
docs.text:
storage.apply_decay_and_archive(decay_lambda, archive_threshold, now) runs in one transaction over memories with status='consolidated'. The current batch is still dreaming at this point, so it is not decayed in its own cycle.

For each row:

anchor = last_accessed if not NULL else created_at
t      = max(0, now - anchor)                 # seconds
w_new  = access_weight * exp(-decay_lambda * t)

If w_new < archive_threshold the row becomes archived, w_new is stored, and all its has_tag edges are deleted. Otherwise w_new is stored.

With the defaults (decay_lambda = 3e-7 per second, archive_threshold = 0.1):

  • One application halves the weight at t = ln 2 / 3e-7, about 2.31 million seconds or 26.7 days.
  • One application crosses 0.1 at t = ln 10 / 3e-7, about 7.68 million seconds or 88.8 days.

The anchor does not move when decay is applied, and each cycle multiplies the already-decayed weight by exp(-lambda * t) again with the full elapsed time. Decay therefore compounds across cycles. For example, with cycles at day 10 and day 20 after creation and no retrieval, the stored weight after the second cycle is exp(-lambda * (10 + 20) days), not exp(-lambda * 20 days). How fast a memory is archived depends on how often dream cycles run.

Archiving removes the memory's has_tag edges. Tag nodes and centroids stay, even if nothing links to them any more.

docs.title: Step 11: status flip
docs.text: The batch goes from dreaming to consolidated in one statement.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If steps 2 to 7, 10 or 11 raise, the except block logs the error, sets the batch back to inbox, and re-raises. If that update also fails it logs "rollback itself failed". The finally block clears is_dreaming and releases the lock.

Rollback only changes status. Each storage call commits on its own, so anything written before the failure stays: summaries, named entities, new tag nodes, centroids, child_of edges and has_tag edges. On the next cycle the same memories are processed again. Summaries are not regenerated because they are no longer empty. has_tag edges are deduplicated by the unique constraint. Clustering runs again over all nodes and writes another set of centroids.

docs.title: ContextHelper.build_prompt_context(task, top_k=5, depth=3)
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q["Task text"] --> V{"Empty text, top_k below 1 or negative depth?"}
    V -->|yes| X["ValueError"]
    V -->|no| E["Embed task (one get_embeddings call)"]
    E --> N["get_nearest_nodes: cosine over all nodes, top_k"]
    N -->|no nodes| R0["Return empty string"]
    N --> S["get_subgraph(seed ids, depth): BFS over child_of in both directions"]
    S --> M["Add has_tag memories of reached nodes, skipping archived"]
    M --> C["_enforce_node_cap: keep seeds, drop farthest nodes above 80"]
    C --> L["resolve_centroid_names, resolve_junction_summaries (normally no-ops)"]
    L --> G{"Any nodes or memories?"}
    G -->|no| R0
    G -->|yes| T["_render_ascii_tree"]
    T --> O["Text tree for the prompt"]
  1. Embed: one embedder.get_embeddings([task]) call; row 0 is the query vector.
  2. Nearest nodes: SQLiteAdapter.get_nearest_nodes loads every node, stacks the embeddings into one matrix, computes cosine similarity with batch_cosine_similarity (zero vectors score 0), and takes the top top_k with argpartition, sorted by similarity. Leaves and centroids compete in the same ranking. This is a full scan with no index.
  3. Subgraph: get_subgraph(seed_ids, depth) does a breadth-first walk over child_of edges in both directions for depth hops. Going both ways means depth 2 from a leaf reaches its parent and its siblings. It then collects has_tag edges that point at any reached node and whose memory is not archived, and loads those memories.
  4. Node cap: _enforce_node_cap does nothing if there are 80 nodes or fewer (_NODE_CAP). Otherwise it computes breadth-first distance from the seeds over child_of edges, sorts nodes by (distance, id) with unreachable nodes last, and keeps the first max(80, number of seeds). Seeds are never dropped. Edges to dropped nodes are removed, and so are memories no longer reachable through a kept has_tag edge.
  5. Lazy resolvers: resolve_centroid_names and resolve_junction_summaries run on the kept nodes. After a completed dream cycle there are no placeholders or empty summaries, so both return without work. If they do find some (for example after step 8 or 9 failed), they log a warning and make the same LLM calls the dream cycle would, so a retrieval can trigger model calls. Neither ever raises.
  6. Render: if the subgraph has no nodes and no memories the result is an empty string. Otherwise _render_ascii_tree.

build_prompt_context does not change access weights. Only retrieve_memories does.

docs.title: Rendering format
docs.text:
_render_ascii_tree:

  • First line: Relevant Memory Context:.
  • Roots are nodes with no child_of parent inside the subgraph, sorted by id.
  • Each node prints as a folder line: the folder emoji (U+1F4C1), a space, and the label. Node ids are not printed.
  • A centroid with a paragraph_summary gets a para: "..." line under it. Summaries longer than 400 characters (_JUNCTION_SUMMARY_MAX_CHARS) are cut to 399 characters plus an ellipsis.
  • Under each node, child nodes come first, then the node's memories (deduplicated within that node).
  • A memory prints as the page emoji (U+1F4C4), the memory id, and the summary in quotes. Summaries longer than 300 characters (_MEMORY_SNIPPET_MAX_CHARS) are cut to 299 plus an ellipsis. raw_content is never rendered.
  • If the memory has tags or entities, a second line follows: tags: a, b · entities: X, Y. Tags are the labels of the nodes in the subgraph that the memory's has_tag edges point to.
  • Tree connectors are ├──, └── and │.
  • A node reached from a second parent prints once more as <label> (also under: <first parent label>), or (also under: top level) if it was first printed as a root, and its subtree is not repeated.
  • Memories are not deduplicated across nodes. A memory linked to three tags in the subgraph is printed three times.
  • No dates are rendered.

Output from _render_ascii_tree on a small subgraph, with the two emoji replaced by [F] (folder) and [M] (memory):

Relevant Memory Context:
[F] education
    para: "The user graduated with a Business Administration degree and now works at Acme Corp."
├── [F] degree
│   └── [M] mem_a1: "The user graduated with a Business Administration degree last year and works at Acme Corp as a junior analyst."
│       tags: degree, Business Administration, Acme Corp · entities: Acme Corp
└── [F] Business Administration
    └── [M] mem_a1: "The user graduated with a Business Administration degree last year and works at Acme Corp as a junior analyst."
        tags: degree, Business Administration, Acme Corp · entities: Acme Corp
[F] career
    para: "Junior analyst role at Acme Corp."
├── [F] Acme Corp
│   └── [M] mem_a1: "The user graduated with a Business Administration degree last year and works at Acme Corp as a junior analyst."
│       tags: degree, Business Administration, Acme Corp · entities: Acme Corp
└── [F] Business Administration (also under: education)

docs.title: LTP spike on retrieve_memories
docs.text:
neuromem.tools.retrieve_memories(memory_ids, system):

  1. Loads each id with get_memory_by_id. Unknown ids are skipped without error.
  2. Collects the ids whose status is consolidated.
  3. Calls spike_access_weight(ids, now) once, which sets access_weight = 1.0 and last_accessed = now for those rows (the SQL also checks status = 'consolidated').
  4. Updates the returned dicts to show the new values.

Memories in inbox, dreaming or archived are returned unchanged and not spiked. An archived memory stays archived and keeps no tag edges. Because the spike moves last_accessed, it also resets the decay anchor.

docs.title: Agent tools
docs.text:
packages/neuromem-core/src/neuromem/tools.py exposes three flat functions that take the NeuroMemory instance as an argument:

Function Arguments and defaults Behaviour search_memory query, top_k=5, depth=2 Calls ContextHelper.build_prompt_context with those values. No LTP. expand_node node_id, depth=2 Clamps depth to 5 (_EXPAND_NODE_MAX_DEPTH), calls get_subgraph([node_id], depth), applies the 80-node cap with node_id as the seed, runs both lazy resolvers and renders. docs.title: Google ADK wiring
docs.text:
neuromem_adk.enable_memory(agent, db_path, *, llm=None, embedder=None, cluster_threshold=None, dream_threshold=None):

  • Creates NeuroMemory(SQLiteAdapter(db_path), llm, embedder). Missing providers default to GeminiLLMProvider and GeminiEmbeddingProvider, with the key read from GOOGLE_API_KEY or GEMINI_API_KEY (a KeyError if neither is set). cluster_threshold and dream_threshold are passed only if given.
  • Appends three tools to agent.tools: search_memory_tool(query, top_k=5, depth=2), retrieve_memories_tool(memory_ids) and expand_node_tool(node_id, depth=2). They are plain wrapper functions, so the model's tool schema does not include the system argument.
  • Adds a before_model_callback. It takes the current user message (or, failing that, the latest user event in the session), calls build_prompt_context(query) with the defaults (top_k=5, depth=3), and appends the tree after the existing system_instruction, separated by a blank line. An empty tree leaves the request unchanged.
  • Adds an after_agent_callback. It calls enqueue twice per turn: once for the user text with metadata {"role": "user", "turn": n} and once for the latest assistant text with {"role": "assistant", "turn": n}, where n is the number of session events. It does not use enqueue_session.
  • Existing callbacks are kept and run before neuromem's. A second call on the same agent raises ValueError.

The rendered tree shows node labels but not node ids, so the model has no id from the tree to pass to expand_node_tool.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
These come from benchmarks/RESULTS.md, the Context section of ADR-005, and the code paths above.

  • Duplicates across tags: a memory is linked to every one of its tags and the renderer prints it under each tag it reaches. ADR-005 found about a third of rendered rows were duplicates, which uses prompt space without adding information.
  • No dates: enqueue_session takes no timestamp, created_at is the insert time, and the render prints no dates. Questions like "how many days ago" cannot be answered, and knowledge-update questions cannot tell an old value from a new one. Knowledge update (0.600) and temporal reasoning (0.667) are among the lowest-scoring types in the stratified run.
  • Label-vector centroids: leaf embeddings are embeddings of 1 to 4 word tag strings, and each centroid is the mean of its children's vectors. ADR-005 notes these drift towards generic centres, so a broad centroid can outrank the specific tag a question needs. RESULTS.md records the "degree" tag ranking behind centroids such as "measurement" and "qualification" at top_k=5.
  • Lossy summaries: retrieval renders only summaries, cut to 300 characters. Summaries are 2 to 4 sentences focused on the user, so details the assistant gave (a list item, a number, a chess move) are lost unless the agent calls retrieve_memories for the raw transcript. RESULTS.md also records a precision miss where two similar memories both appeared and the summaries did not distinguish them.
  • Graph growth: each cycle clusters all existing nodes again, including old centroids, and never deletes centroids, so the hierarchy gains layers and multi-parent nodes over time. Junction summaries of existing centroids are not refreshed when new memories are linked to the tags beneath them.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
The pre-fix benchmark on a single instance (e47becba, the degree question) had regressed to 0.00 after PRs #51 / #52 / #54 merged (concurrent ingestion, per-session summarisation, lazy centroid naming). Root-caused through a 3-stage diagnostic (packages/neuromem-bench/scripts/diag_instance1_full.py):

Stage Check Result before fix A — summarisation Does any memory's summary contain "Business Administration"? flaky: sometimes yes, often no B — retrieval Is the fact in the rendered context tree? flaky: ~20% miss rate even when stage A passed C — answer Does the LLM answer correctly given the tree? deterministic given tree contents

Two distinct failure modes, both fixed independently:

  1. Stage A — fact-preserving summarisation & tagging (packages/neuromem-gemini/src/neuromem_gemini/llm.py). Per-session summarisation (PR #52) compresses ~18K-char multi-turn sessions into 2–4 sentence summaries. The previous prompt ("summarise, preserve proper nouns") biased the LLM toward the dominant topic and dropped briefly-mentioned personal facts — "I graduated with a degree in Business Administration" routinely lost to "here are some task-management apps I'd recommend". Rewrote generate_summary and extract_tags / extract_tags_batch with:
  2. Explicit fact-preservation instructions (personal facts, proper nouns, numbers/dates, implied facts).
  3. Explicit bias correction: "a summary that omits a brand list is fine; a summary that omits 'I graduated with Business Administration' has FAILED."
  4. Worked GOOD/BAD examples so the model pattern-matches rather than improvises.

  5. Bumped the tag cap from 3–5 → 5–12 for tag extraction. The old cap forced the LLM to pick dominant topics under artificial scarcity; session-level summaries need enough tag slots to anchor every fact the user might later ask about.

  6. Stage B — retrieval cliff (packages/neuromem-bench/src/neuromem_bench/agent.py). ContextHelper.build_prompt_context seeds the subgraph walk with top_k=5 nearest tag/centroid nodes to the question embedding, then renders depth-2 neighbours. For the degree question, the "degree" tag node sometimes ranked 6+ behind generic centroids like "measurement", "learning", "qualification" — falling off the cliff and making the memory invisible to the answer LLM even though it existed in storage. Bumping the agent's call to top_k=20 widens the seed set enough that the relevant tag stays reachable. Still cheap (20 nearest over hundreds of nodes is a sub-ms numpy operation; the expanded subgraph walk is depth-bounded).

1. Instance 2 is the money shot. NullAgent refuses because the fact is outside its 50-turn window. NeuromemAgent retrieves it from the concept graph and answers correctly. This is exactly the use case neuromem exists for.

Per-instance cost driven by: - ~160 generate_summary calls on the enqueue hot path (1 per turn) - 1 batched extract_tags call (#45 fix — previously 160 serial calls) - ~20-40 generate_category_name calls during agglomerative clustering (inherently serial — each merge depends on the previous) - 1 final answer call with injected memory context

The ~87-min runtime for 3 instances is manageable for a baseline-measurement benchmark but becomes impractical at LongMemEval's full 500-instance scale (~240 hours). Sampling to 25-50 instances gives statistical signal within a few hours.

docs.title: Known follow-ups
docs.text:
1. Prompt-tune extract_tags to prioritise named entities (instance 3's "Target" loss). Currently the prompt says "exclude stopwords" but doesn't positively instruct the LLM to preserve proper nouns. Cheap fix, likely significant quality lift.
  2. Issue #42 — clustering quality (duplicate centroid names, recursive subtrees). Not on the benchmark critical path but affects graph readability.
  3. Batch generate_category_name similar to how #45 batched extract_tags. Each merge step depends on prior merges so strict batching is impossible, but we could batch "initial centroid naming" where multiple independent clusters are named simultaneously. Would cut another ~50% of dream-cycle latency.
  4. Scale up the benchmark — rerun at n=25 or n=50 once the prompt tuning lands, to get statistical confidence beyond a 3-instance anecdote.
